title: Kernel and cokernel killed by K^t: the maps "fg" and reduction modulo an ideal
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $\mathfrak K\subseteq A$ an ideal, $t\ge1$ an integer, and $u:M\to N$ an $A$-linear map of $A$-modules such that $\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Ker}(u)=0$ and $\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Coker}(u)=0$, where $\operatorname{Coker}(u)=N/u(M)$ (equivalently: there is an exact sequence $0\to T\to M\xrightarrow{u}N\to Q\to0$ of $A$-modules with $\mathfrak K^tT=\mathfrak K^tQ=0$). (a) For all $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$ and every $y\in N$ there is $x\in M$ with $u(x)=fy$, and $gx$ does not depend on the choice of $x$; the resulting map $h_{f,g}=\text{``}fg\text{''}:N\to M$, $y\mapsto gx$, is $A$-linear and satisfies $h_{f,g}\circ u=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_M$ and $u\circ h_{f,g}=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_N$. (b) (Naturality.) If $u':M'\to N'$ is another $A$-linear map with $\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Ker}(u')=\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Coker}(u')=0$ and $a:M\to M'$, $b:N\to N'$ are $A$-linear maps with $u'\circ a=b\circ u$, then $a\circ h_{f,g}=h'_{f,g}\circ b$ for all $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$, where $h'_{f,g}$ is the map of (a) for $u'$. (c) For every ideal $J\subseteq A$ the kernel and the cokernel of the induced map $\bar u:M/JM\to N/JN$ are annihilated by $\mathfrak K^{2t}$. (d) (Converse criterion.) Let $v:P\to R$ be any $A$-linear map of $A$-modules such that for all $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$ there is an $A$-linear map $k:R\to P$ with $k\circ v=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_P$ and $v\circ k=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_R$. Then $\operatorname{Ker}(v)$ and $\operatorname{Coker}(v)$ are annihilated by $\mathfrak K^{2t}$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), the commutative algebra fact of its proof (lines 6915-6928: the maps "fg": N -> M and the annihilation by K^{2t} modulo J); the naturality (b) and the converse criterion (d) are the facts the limit argument of the same remark (lines 6930-6936) uses, stated by an agent

proof.text: (Conventions; the exact-sequence form of the hypothesis.) For an $A$-module $X$ and an ideal $\mathfrak a\subseteq A$, $\mathfrak aX=0$ means $ax=0$ for all $a\in\mathfrak a$, $x\in X$; $\mathfrak K^t$ is the ideal generated by the products $k_1\cdots k_t$ with $k_i\in\mathfrak K$, and $JM$ is the submodule of finite sums $\sum j_im_i$ ($j_i\in J$, $m_i\in M$). If $\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Ker}(u)=\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Coker}(u)=0$, then $0\to\operatorname{Ker}(u)\to M\xrightarrow{u}N\to N/u(M)\to0$ (inclusion, $u$, projection) is exact [def-weil-pbc-exact-sequence]: the inclusion is injective with image $\operatorname{Ker}(u)$, the image of $u$ is $u(M)$, the kernel of the projection, and the projection is surjective; so $T=\operatorname{Ker}(u)$, $Q=\operatorname{Coker}(u)$ will do. Conversely, given an exact sequence $0\to T\xrightarrow{i}M\xrightarrow{u}N\xrightarrow{p}Q\to0$, $i$ is injective with image $\operatorname{Ker}(u)$, so $i:T\to\operatorname{Ker}(u)$ is an $A$-linear bijection, and $p$ is surjective with kernel $u(M)$, so it induces an $A$-linear bijection $N/u(M)\to Q$; an $A$-linear bijection $X\cong Y$ carries $ax$ to $a\cdot(\text{image of }x)$, so $\mathfrak K^tT=0\iff\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Ker}(u)=0$ and $\mathfrak K^tQ=0\iff\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Coker}(u)=0$.

proof.text: ((a), existence of $x$.) Let $f\in\mathfrak K^t$ and $y\in N$. The class $\bar y\in\operatorname{Coker}(u)=N/u(M)$ satisfies $f\bar y=\overline{fy}$, and $f\bar y=0$ because $\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Coker}(u)=0$. Hence $fy\in u(M)$: there is $x\in M$ with $u(x)=fy$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), lines 6920-6922 ('for y in N we can pick x in M mapping to fy in N')

proof.text: ((a), $gx$ does not depend on $x$.) Let $g\in\mathfrak K^t$ and let $x,x'\in M$ with $u(x)=u(x')=fy$. Then $u(x-x')=0$, so $x-x'\in\operatorname{Ker}(u)$, and $g(x-x')=0$ because $\mathfrak K^t\operatorname{Ker}(u)=0$; thus $gx=gx'$. So $h_{f,g}(y)=gx$, for any $x$ with $u(x)=fy$, is a well-defined map $N\to M$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), lines 6922-6923 ('and then we can set "fg"(y) = gx'); the independence of the choice, which the source leaves implicit in 'canonical', written out by an agent

proof.text: ((a), $h_{f,g}$ is $A$-linear.) Let $y_1,y_2\in N$, $a\in A$, and choose $x_1,x_2\in M$ with $u(x_1)=fy_1$, $u(x_2)=fy_2$. Then $u(x_1+x_2)=f(y_1+y_2)$ and $u(ax_1)=au(x_1)=f(ay_1)$, so $x_1+x_2$ and $ax_1$ are admissible choices for $y_1+y_2$ and $ay_1$; by Step 2, $h_{f,g}(y_1+y_2)=g(x_1+x_2)=h_{f,g}(y_1)+h_{f,g}(y_2)$ and $h_{f,g}(ay_1)=g(ax_1)=a\,h_{f,g}(y_1)$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), line 6919 ('a canonical map "fg": N -> M'; linearity written out by an agent)

proof.text: ((a), the two composites.) For $m\in M$: $u(fm)=f\,u(m)$, so $x=fm$ is an admissible choice for $y=u(m)$, and $h_{f,g}(u(m))=gfm=fg\,m$; thus $h_{f,g}\circ u=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_M$. For $y\in N$ with $x$ chosen as in Step 1: $u(h_{f,g}(y))=u(gx)=g\,u(x)=gfy=fg\,y$; thus $u\circ h_{f,g}=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_N$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), lines 6919-6920 ('such that M -> N -> M is equal to multiplication by fg'); the other composite N -> M -> N written out by an agent (the source uses it at line 6934)

proof.text: ((b), naturality.) Let $u',a,b$ be as in (b), $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$ and $y\in N$; choose $x\in M$ with $u(x)=fy$ (Step 1). Then $u'(a(x))=b(u(x))=b(fy)=f\,b(y)$, so $a(x)$ is an admissible choice for the element $b(y)$ of $N'$ in the definition of $h'_{f,g}$ (which is defined by Steps 1-3 applied to $u'$, whose kernel and cokernel are killed by $\mathfrak K^t$). Hence $h'_{f,g}(b(y))=g\,a(x)=a(gx)=a(h_{f,g}(y))$, i.e. $a\circ h_{f,g}=h'_{f,g}\circ b$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), lines 6930-6933 (the maps "fg": N/I^nN -> M/I^nM 'in the limit induce a map N -> M', which needs their compatibility with the transition maps); stated and proved by an agent

proof.text: ((d), converse criterion.) Let $v:P\to R$ be as in (d) and $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$, with $k:R\to P$, $k\circ v=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_P$, $v\circ k=fg\cdot\mathrm{id}_R$. If $p\in\operatorname{Ker}(v)$ then $fg\,p=k(v(p))=k(0)=0$. If $r\in R$ then $fg\,r=v(k(r))\in v(P)$, so $fg\,\bar r=0$ in $\operatorname{Coker}(v)=R/v(P)$. So every product $fg$ ($f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$) kills $\operatorname{Ker}(v)$ and $\operatorname{Coker}(v)$. Now $\mathfrak K^{2t}=\mathfrak K^t\mathfrak K^t$ (a product of $2t$ elements of $\mathfrak K$ is a product of two products of $t$ elements; conversely a product of two finite sums of products of $t$ elements times elements of $A$ expands into a sum of $A$-multiples of products of $2t$ elements), and every element of $\mathfrak K^t\mathfrak K^t$ is a finite sum $\sum_i f_ig_i$ with $f_i,g_i\in\mathfrak K^t$. Since the annihilator of a module is closed under sums, $\mathfrak K^{2t}$ kills $\operatorname{Ker}(v)$ and $\operatorname{Coker}(v)$.

source.place: Cohomology of Schemes, Remark 0888 (remark-inverse-systems-kernel-cokernel-annihilated-by, line 6887), lines 6933-6936 ('Since the composition with N -> M -> N is multiplication by fg we conclude that fg annihilates T and Q. In other words T and Q are annihilated by K^{2t}'); the passage from the products fg to the ideal K^{2t} written out by an agent

proof.text: ((c), reduction modulo $J$.) Let $J\subseteq A$ be an ideal and $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$, $h=h_{f,g}$ (Steps 1-4). As $u$ and $h$ are $A$-linear, $u(\sum j_im_i)=\sum j_iu(m_i)\in JN$ and $h(\sum j_iy_i)=\sum j_ih(y_i)\in JM$; so $u(JM)\subseteq JN$, $h(JN)\subseteq JM$, and $u,h$ induce $A$-linear maps $\bar u:M/JM\to N/JN$, $\bar x\mapsto\overline{u(x)}$, and $\bar h:N/JN\to M/JM$, $\bar y\mapsto\overline{h(y)}$. By Step 4, $\bar h(\bar u(\bar x))=\overline{h(u(x))}=\overline{fg\,x}=fg\,\bar x$ and $\bar u(\bar h(\bar y))=\overline{u(h(y))}=fg\,\bar y$. So $v=\bar u$ satisfies the hypothesis of (d) with $k=\bar h$ for every pair $f,g\in\mathfrak K^t$, and by Step 6 $\operatorname{Ker}(\bar u)$ and $\operatorname{Coker}(\bar u)$ are annihilated by $\mathfrak K^{2t}$.

lean.statement: theorem ker_coker_annihilated_mod_ideal {A : Type u} [CommRing A] {M : Type v} {N : Type v'} [AddCommGroup M] [Module A M] [AddCommGroup N] [Module A N] (K : Ideal A) (t : ℕ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) (u : M →ₗ[A] N) (hker : K ^ t ≤ Module.annihilator A (ker u)) (hcoker : K ^ t ≤ Module.annihilator A (N ⧸ range u)) : (∀ (f g : A), f ∈ K ^ t → g ∈ K ^ t → (∀ y : N, ∃ x : M, u x = f • y) ∧ (∀ (y : N) (x x' : M), u x = f • y → u x' = f • y → g • x = g • x') ∧ ∃ h : N →ₗ[A] M, (∀ (y : N) (x : M), u x = f • y → h y = g • x) ∧ h.comp u = (f * g) • LinearMap.id ∧ u.comp h = (f * g) • LinearMap.id ∧ ∀ (M' : Type w) (N' : Type w') [AddCommGroup M'] [Module A M'] [AddCommGroup N'] [Module A N'] (u' : M' →ₗ[A] N'), K ^ t ≤ Module.annihilator A (ker u') → K ^ t ≤ Module.annihilator A (N' ⧸ range u') → ∀ (a : M →ₗ[A] M') (b : N →ₗ[A] N') (h' : N' →ₗ[A] M'), u'.comp a = b.comp u → (∀ (y : N') (x : M'), u' x = f • y → h' y = g • x) → a.comp h = h'.comp b) ∧ (∀ J : Ideal A, let ū := (J • ⊤ : Submodule A M).mapQ (J • ⊤ : Submodule A N) u (Submodule.smul_top_le_comap_smul_top J u) K ^ (2 * t) ≤ Module.annihilator A (ker ū) ∧ K ^ (2 * t) ≤ Module.annihilator A ((N ⧸ (J • ⊤ : Submodule A N)) ⧸ range ū)) ∧ (∀ (P : Type z) (R : Type z') [AddCommGroup P] [Module A P] [AddCommGroup R] [Module A R] (v : P →ₗ[A] R), (∀ (f g : A), f ∈ K ^ t → g ∈ K ^ t → ∃ k : R →ₗ[A] P, k.comp v = (f * g) • LinearMap.id ∧ v.comp k = (f * g) • LinearMap.id) → K ^ (2 * t) ≤ Module.annihilator A (ker v) ∧ K ^ (2 * t) ≤ Module.annihilator A (R ⧸ range v))
